questions.question: Which statement best captures an essential characteristic of an embedded system as emphasized in the design challenge and processor constraints?

options.A: It must be capable of running multiple unrelated applications simultaneously.
options.B: It is typically designed to perform a dedicated, single‑purpose function.
options.C: It always uses a general‑purpose processor without any custom hardware.
options.D: It relies exclusively on external memory for program storage.

questions.explanation:
The starter activity (page 36) asks groups to design a “basic embedded system” and the constraints (page 4) highlight “Design of Custom Single Purpose Processor,” indicating that embedded systems are usually built for a specific, dedicated task.

---

questions.question: How does the definition of a microcontroller (MCU) on page 43 differentiate it from a microprocessor (MPU)?

options.A: An MCU combines CPU, memory, and I/O on a single chip, whereas an MPU provides only the CPU.
options.B: An MPU integrates CPU, memory, and I/O on one chip, while an MCU requires external peripherals.
options.C: Both MCU and MPU are identical; the terms are interchangeable.
options.D: An MCU can only execute firmware, whereas an MPU can run full operating systems.

questions.explanation:
Page 43 lists the feature that an MCU “CPU + memory + I/O on one chip,” while an MPU is “CPU only; needs external memory.”

---

questions.question: Which processing‑core category described on page 40 is explicitly optimized for a particular application domain?

options.B: Domain‑Specific Processors such as DSPs, ASIPs, and SSPs
options.C: Multi‑core CPUs used in desktop computers

questions.explanation:
Page 40 states that “Domain‑Specific Processors (DSPs / ASIP / SSP) – Optimized for a particular application or domain.”

---

questions.question: According to the starter activity (page 36), which combination correctly represents the three functional blocks of a basic embedded system?

options.A: Power supply, wireless module, cloud server

questions.explanation:
The activity instructs groups to identify “Inputs (Sensors) … Processing Unit … Outputs (Actuators)” as the core components of an embedded system.

---

questions.question: Why can Commercial‑Off‑The‑Shelf (COTS) platforms such as Arduino or Raspberry Pi still satisfy embedded‑system design constraints, based on the context (pages 39‑40)?

options.A: They are always cheaper than custom ASICs, regardless of performance.
options.B: They provide ready‑made hardware and software ecosystems that can be tailored to single‑purpose tasks.
options.C: They are required to use only general‑purpose processors, which eliminates real‑time capability.
options.D: They cannot be used in embedded applications because they lack any processing core.

questions.explanation:
Pages 39‑40 list Arduino, Raspberry Pi, ESP32 as COTS options, implying that such platforms can be repurposed for specific embedded functions while leveraging existing resources.

---

questions.question: How does the “single‑purpose design” characteristic influence the choice of processor for an embedded system, as discussed on page 4?

options.A: Designers prefer high‑end CPUs to allow future feature expansion.
options.B: A custom single‑purpose processor or a domain‑specific core is selected to meet the dedicated task efficiently.
options.C: The system must use a general‑purpose microprocessor to ensure flexibility.
options.D: The processor choice is irrelevant because software can compensate for any hardware.

questions.explanation:
Page 4 lists “Design of Custom Single Purpose Processor” among the constraints, indicating that a dedicated processor is chosen to match the single‑purpose nature of the system.

---

questions.question: In a temperature‑monitoring embedded system that uses a temperature sensor, an Arduino MCU, and an LED indicator, how is the characteristic of “real‑time operation” reflected?

options.A: The system stores all temperature readings for later batch processing.
options.B: The LED updates immediately after each sensor reading, providing instant feedback.
options.C: The Arduino sends data to a remote server for delayed analysis.
options.D: The system requires user interaction before displaying any temperature value.

questions.explanation:
Real‑time operation means the system responds promptly to inputs; the context’s emphasis on inputs, processing, and outputs (page 36) supports immediate LED response as an example.

---

questions.question: Which option best illustrates the “resource‑constrained” nature of embedded systems as described across the provided material?

options.A: Unlimited RAM and storage are assumed for all designs.
options.B: The system must operate with limited memory, power, and processing capability.
options.C: Designers can freely add any number of peripherals without cost concerns.
options.D: Embedded systems always run on desktop‑class CPUs.

questions.explanation:
Throughout the context (e.g., pages 36, 40, 43) embedded systems are portrayed as having tight constraints on memory, power, and processing resources.

---

questions.question: Based on the classification information (page 20) and core types (page 40), an embedded system that employs a TI C6000 DSP for audio signal processing would be classified primarily as which type?
questions.explanation:
Page 20 discusses classification, while page 40 identifies DSPs as “Domain‑Specific Processors,” making the audio‑DSP system fall into that category.

---

questions.question: Which scenario best demonstrates the embedded‑system principle of tight integration between hardware and software, using the elements listed on page 38?

options.A: A desktop PC running a word processor while using a separate external hard drive.
options.B: A microcontroller that directly reads sensor data, processes it with firmware, and drives an actuator without an operating system.
options.C: A smartphone that downloads apps from an app store and runs them in a multitasking OS.
options.D: A cloud server that processes data sent from numerous remote devices.

questions.explanation: Page 38 outlines elements such as sensors, processing unit, and actuators, emphasizing that an embedded system tightly couples hardware (sensor/actuator) with firmware on the processing unit.
